This note investigates the collision time \(\tau\) of \(n\) independent Brownian motions with respective drifts \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), started from strictly ordered positions \(x_1<\cdots<x_n\). Its main objective is to determine the precise long-time behavior of the probability that no two particles have collided by time \(t\). Specifically, it establishes the asymptotic formula
\[
P_x(\tau>t)=C\,h(x)\,t^{-\alpha}e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr),
\qquad t\to\infty.
\]
Here, the constant \(C\), the function \(h(x)\), the polynomial decay exponent \(\alpha\), and the exponential decay rate \(\gamma\) are all identified explicitly in terms of the drift parameters \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\). Thus, the result provides an exact description of how the initial configuration and the relative drifts determine the long-time probability of avoiding collisions.

Let \(X_i(t)=x_i+\mu_i t+B_i(t)\), \(1\le i\le n\), be independent one-dimensional Brownian motions started from distinct ordered points \(x_1<\cdots <x_n\), with arbitrary real drifts \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n\). Denote by  
\[
\tau=\inf\{t>0:X_i(t)=X_j(t)\text{ for some }i\ne j\}
\]
their first collision time. Equivalently, \(\tau\) is the first exit time of the vector process \(X(t)\) from the Weyl chamber
\[
W=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:y_1<\cdots <y_n\}.
\]

The note determines the precise long-time behavior of the noncollision probability \(P_x(\tau>t)\). Using the Karlin–McGregor determinant for Brownian motion killed on the boundary of \(W\), together with a change of measure that incorporates the drifts, the survival probability is reduced to an asymptotic analysis of a determinantal integral. The drift vector is then decomposed into ordered blocks, or equivalently projected onto the cone of nondecreasing vectors. This decomposition captures whether neighboring particles tend to separate, move together, or approach one another, and it governs every term in the final asymptotic formula.

For every choice of distinct starting positions and arbitrary drifts, including repeated drifts and drifts that are not ordered consistently with the initial particle positions, the result has the form
\[
P_x(\tau>t)
   =C\,h(x)\,t^{-\alpha}e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr),
   \qquad t\to\infty.
\]
Here \(\gamma\ge0\) is the exponential decay rate and measures the large-deviation cost required for the particles to maintain their order. It is determined by the distance of the drift vector from the closed cone of nondecreasing drifts. The exponent \(\alpha\ge0\) is the polynomial correction arising from groups of particles whose effective asymptotic velocities coincide and from degeneracies at the minimizing boundary point. The function \(h(x)\) is a positive space-dependent factor obtained from the relevant determinant, while \(C>0\) is an explicit normalization constant. All four quantities are expressed directly in terms of the drift block structure.

The formula unifies the different qualitative regimes. If the drifts are strictly increasing in the order of the particles, collisions are not forced asymptotically, and the noncollision probability converges to a positive limit, corresponding to \(\alpha=\gamma=0\). If some effective drifts coincide, the decay is polynomial; in particular, when all drifts are equal one recovers the classical exponent \(n(n-1)/4\). If the drift configuration pushes one or more particles toward those ahead of them, the survival probability is exponentially small, with an additional polynomial factor reflecting the geometry of the associated drift blocks.

Thus the result gives more than the logarithmic decay rate: it provides the full leading asymptotic, including the exact exponential rate, power of \(t\), dependence on the starting configuration, and multiplicative constant. It extends the classical noncolliding Brownian-motion asymptotics to completely general drift configurations and makes explicit how the ordering and multiplicities of the drifts determine the long-time probability of avoiding collision.

# Brownian Motion

Brownian motion is the continuous, random movement of tiny particles suspended in a liquid or gas. The phenomenon is named after Scottish botanist Robert Brown, who observed pollen particles moving unpredictably in water in 1827. Although Brown initially wondered whether the motion was linked to life, he later found that non-living particles behaved in the same way.

The movement occurs because suspended particles are constantly struck by the rapidly moving molecules of the surrounding fluid. These collisions happen unevenly, causing each particle to follow an irregular, zigzag path. In 1905, Albert Einstein developed a mathematical explanation of Brownian motion that provided strong evidence for the existence of atoms and molecules.

Today, Brownian motion is important in many scientific fields. In physics and chemistry, it helps researchers understand diffusion and molecular behavior. In biology, it describes the movement of microscopic substances inside cells. Similar mathematical models are also used in finance to represent unpredictable changes in asset prices, although real markets are more complex than ideal Brownian systems.

Brownian motion demonstrates how countless microscopic interactions can create visible randomness. It connects the hidden molecular world with observable phenomena and remains a fundamental concept in probability, statistics, and modern science.

counterfactuals.output:
Let \(X_i(t)=x_i+a_i t+B_i(t)\), where the \(B_i\) are independent standard Brownian motions, \(x_1<\cdots <x_n\), and
\[
\tau=\inf\{t\ge 0:X_1(t)\ge X_2(t)\ \text{for some adjacent pair}\}.
\]
The paper derives the precise long-time asymptotic of \(P_x(\tau>t)\) for an arbitrary drift vector \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\).

The key object is the Euclidean projection
\[
f=\Pi_{\overline W}a,\qquad 
\overline W=\{z_1\le\cdots\le z_n\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(f\) is obtained by isotonic regression of the drifts: adjacent groups whose average drifts are in the wrong order are repeatedly pooled. Thus
\[
f=(\underbrace{c_1,\ldots,c_1}_{\nu_1},
   \underbrace{c_2,\ldots,c_2}_{\nu_2},\ldots,
   \underbrace{c_m,\ldots,c_m}_{\nu_m}),
\qquad c_1<\cdots<c_m.
\]
These maximal constant groups are the stable blocks. Inside them, the paper introduces a finer “irreducible” partition, determined by the contact points of the cumulative-drift polygon with the chord joining the block’s endpoints. If \(q\) is the total number of irreducible subblocks, then
\[
\boxed{\gamma=\frac12\lVert a-f\rVert^2}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\alpha=\frac12\sum_{k=1}^m\binom{\nu_k}{2}+n-q}.
\]

The spatial factor is an explicit positive eigenfunction of the killed generator. With columns indexed by pairs \((k,r)\), \(1\le r\le\nu_k\), it can be normalized as
\[
h_a(x)=e^{-\langle a,x\rangle}
\det\!\left[
   \frac{x_i^{\,r-1}}{(r-1)!}e^{c_kx_i}
\right]_{\substack{1\le i\le n\\(k,r)}} ,
\]
with the column order chosen so that the determinant is positive on
\(W=\{x_1<\cdots <x_n\}\). Multiplying \(h_a\) by a fixed scalar merely changes \(C\).

The main theorem is
\[
\boxed{
P_x(\tau>t)
 =C(a)\,h_a(x)\,t^{-\alpha}e^{-\gamma t}(1+o(1)),
 \qquad t\to\infty .
}
\]
The constant \(C(a)>0\) is also given explicitly in the paper. It is assembled from the stable/irreducible partition: powers of \(2\pi\), factorial and Gamma factors coming from confluent Vandermonde determinants and Gaussian–Vandermonde integrals, and linear drift-gap factors determined by the cumulative drift excesses inside each irreducible block. Hence no undetermined spectral constant remains; once the block decomposition of \(a\) is known, \(C,\alpha,\gamma\), and \(h\) are all computable.

The proof starts from the Karlin–McGregor determinant for Brownian motion killed at the boundary of the Weyl chamber. After factoring out the drift, a constrained Laplace analysis shows that the dominant velocity is \(f\). The distance from \(a\) to the ordered cone produces \(e^{-\gamma t}\); confluent determinant expansions within equal-\(f\) blocks produce the Vandermonde part of \(h\) and the term \(\frac12\sum_k\binom{\nu_k}{2}\); and directions in which the Laplace maximum lies on a proper face contribute the additional power \(n-q\).

The formula neatly separates the regimes:

- If \(a_1<\cdots<a_n\), then \(f=a\), \(\gamma=\alpha=0\), and the non-collision probability converges to a positive limit.
- If all drifts are equal, then \(f=a\), \(q=n\), and
  \[
  \alpha=\frac{n(n-1)}4,
  \]
  recovering the classical driftless power law.
- If some drift inequalities are reversed, \(\gamma>0\), so survival is exponentially unlikely, with a polynomial correction determined by the geometry of the pooled drift blocks.

counterfactuals.output:
Let \(X_i(t)=x_i+a_i t+B_i(t)\), with \(x_1<\cdots <x_n\), and let  
\[
\tau=\inf\{t>0:X_i(t)=X_j(t)\text{ for some }i\ne j\}.
\]
The principal result is that, for arbitrary unequal drifts,
\[
\mathbb P_x(\tau>t)\sim C(a)\,h_a(x)\,t^{-\alpha}
   \exp\!\left[-\frac12\,\operatorname{dist}(a,\overline W)^2t\right],
   \qquad t\to\infty,
\]
where \(\overline W=\{z_1\le\cdots\le z_n\}\), and the drift vector \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) is projected onto this ordered cone.

If that projection has constant blocks of sizes \(\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_q\), then
\[
\alpha=\frac12\sum_{k=1}^q\binom{\nu_k}{2}.
\]
Here \(C(a)>0\) is explicit and \(h_a(x)\) is an explicit positive determinant/confluent-determinant function.

Thus the projection determines the exponential decay, while its block structure determines the polynomial correction. In particular, if \(a_1<\cdots<a_n\), the particles drift apart and the survival probability tends to a positive limit; inversions in the drift ordering produce exponential decay.

\begin{abstract}
We study the collision time \(\tau\) of independent one-dimensional Brownian motions started from an ordered configuration \(x\) and killed upon exiting the corresponding Weyl chamber. Exact large-time survival asymptotics take the form
\[
\mathbb P_x(\tau>t)
  = C\,h(x)\,t^{-\alpha}e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr),
  \qquad t\to\infty,
\]
where \(h\) is the relevant positive harmonic or ground-state function, \(\alpha\) is a chamber-dependent polynomial exponent, and \(\gamma\) is the spectral decay rate induced by the drift. In the driftless type-\(A\) case with \(n\) particles,
\[
h(x)=\prod_{1\le i<j\le n}(x_j-x_i),\qquad
\alpha=\frac{n(n-1)}{4},\qquad \gamma=0.
\]
These formulas identify both the universal Vandermonde repulsion and the precise polynomial--exponential decay of long-time non-collision probabilities.
\end{abstract}
